title: Dido saucia. Anna. Iunonis consilium
titleEn: Dido's Wound, Anna's Counsel and Juno's Offer — Aeneid IV.1–104
part: Dido's Wound, Anna's Counsel and Juno's Offer (IV.1–104)
about: Book IV opens on the queen of Carthage. Dido is wounded by love for Aeneas and cannot sleep: his courage, his lineage, his words and his face keep returning to her. At dawn she confesses it to her sister Anna. She believes he is of divine stock; she had resolved never to take a second husband after Sychaeus was murdered; and yet this man alone has shaken her resolve. She would sooner be swallowed by the earth than break faith with Shame. Anna answers that she is wasting her youth for the dead, reminds her of the hostile peoples around Carthage and of her brother's threats from Tyre, and says that the gods and Juno must have brought the Trojans here. She tells Dido to sacrifice, to be hospitable, and to keep the guest from sailing while winter holds the sea. Her words inflame Dido further. The two women make sacrifice, above all to Juno, guardian of marriage, but vows and shrines cannot cure the silent wound. Dido wanders the city like a wounded deer with the arrow still in her flank, makes Aeneas tell his tale again and again, and lets the building of Carthage stop. Juno sees it, and proposes a bargain to Venus with bitter irony: let the two of them rule both peoples together, Dido married to the Trojan and the Tyrians given as her dowry.

sentences.t:
At regina gravi iamdudum saucia cura
volnus alit venis, et caeco carpitur igni.
sentences.l:
But the queen, by heavy care long since wounded,
feeds a wound in her veins, and is plucked at by a blind fire.
sentences.i: But the queen, long since wounded by a heavy care, nurses the hurt in her veins and is consumed by a hidden fire.
sentences.n: The book opens on Dido, whom the reader last saw at the end of Book I falling in love; this line also begins one of Greenough's paragraphs. 'regina' is the subject; 'saucia' (wounded) agrees with it; 'gravi cura' is an ablative of cause, 'by heavy care'. 'iamdudum' is an adverb, 'for a long time now'. Love is a wound and a fire, the two images that run through the whole book. 'caeco igni' — 'blind' means hidden, unseen. 'carpitur' is passive: she is plucked at, worn away. 'volnus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulnus'.

sentences.t:
Multa viri virtus animo, multusque recursat
gentis honos:
sentences.l:
Much of the man's courage to her mind, and much
of his race's honour runs back:
sentences.i: Again and again the man's courage comes back to her mind, and the great honour of his race:
sentences.n: 'multa… virtus' and 'multus… honos' — each adjective agrees with its noun and means 'much' (an abundance of); 'recursat' is a frequentative of 'recurro', 'keeps running back', with one verb serving both subjects. 'animo' is 'to her mind'. 'viri' is Aeneas, not named. The colon introduces what is meant by this: his looks and his words stay with her.

sentences.t:
haerent infixi pectore voltus
verbaque, nec placidam membris dat cura quietem.
sentences.l:
cling, fixed in her breast, his looks
and words, nor does care give calm rest to her limbs.
sentences.i: His looks and his words stay fixed in her heart, and care will not give her limbs peaceful rest.
sentences.n: 'haerent' is plural with two subjects, 'voltus' (Greenough's spelling of 'vultus', looks, features) and 'verba'; 'infixi' is masculine and agrees with 'voltus', serving for 'verba' as well. 'pectore' is an ablative of place, 'in her breast'. 'dat' is singular with its own subject 'cura'. 'nec' here means 'and not'. 'membris' is dative, 'to her limbs'.

sentences.t:
Postera Phoebea lustrabat lampade terras,
umentemque Aurora polo dimoverat umbram,
cum sic unanimam adloquitur male sana sororem:
sentences.l:
The next dawn was travelling the lands with Phoebus's lamp,
and Aurora from the sky had moved away the dewy shade,
when thus her one-souled sister she addresses, ill in her mind:
sentences.i: The next Dawn was lighting the earth with the lamp of Phoebus and had swept the damp shadow from the sky, when, scarcely in her right mind, she speaks thus to the sister who shares her heart:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and a time-marker in the epic manner: 'Postera' (the following) goes with 'Aurora' in the next line, Dawn personified. 'Phoebea lampade' — the lamp of Phoebus, the Sun. 'lustrabat' and 'dimoverat' are imperfect and pluperfect, and 'cum' with the present 'adloquitur' means 'when': the main action arrives in the last line. 'umentem' is 'humentem', damp, dewy. 'unanimam' (one-souled) shows how close the sisters are. 'polo' is an ablative of separation, 'from the sky'. 'male sana' is 'ill in mind', hardly sane.

sentences.t: “Anna soror, quae me suspensam insomnia terrent!
sentences.l: “Anna, sister, what sleepless nights terrify me in suspense!
sentences.i: “Anna, my sister, what sleepless terrors hold me in dread suspense!
sentences.n: Dido's speech opens (the marks run to line 29). 'quae' is the exclamatory adjective 'what', agreeing with 'insomnia', here troubled wakeful nights or visions. 'suspensam' agrees with 'me': hanging, uncertain.

sentences.t:
Quis novus hic nostris successit sedibus hospes,
quem sese ore ferens, quam forti pectore et armis!
sentences.l:
Who this new guest has come to our dwellings,
what a man bearing himself in his face, how brave in heart and arms!
sentences.i: Who is this stranger who has come to our home — what a bearing in his face, what a brave heart, what prowess in arms!
sentences.n: She does not name Aeneas. 'Quis… hic hospes' is the question; then the question turns to exclamation: 'quem' (what a man) and 'quam' (how). 'sese ore ferens' — carrying himself in his face; 'ore' is his countenance. 'successit' takes the dative 'sedibus', 'came into our dwellings'. 'hospes' means guest and stranger at once.

sentences.t: Credo equidem, nec vana fides, genus esse deorum.
sentences.l: I believe indeed — nor is the trust vain — his race to be of gods.
sentences.i: I do believe — and my belief is no empty one — that he is of the race of the gods.
sentences.n: 'credo' takes an accusative and infinitive: 'genus esse deorum', 'that his race is of gods'. 'nec vana fides' is a parenthesis, 'and the belief is not empty'. Aeneas is in fact the son of Venus. 'deorum' is the ordinary genitive plural; compare the older 'divom' that Greenough prints at line 95.

sentences.t: Degeneres animos timor arguit:
sentences.l: Degenerate spirits fear proves:
sentences.i: Fear proves a spirit base-born:
sentences.n: 'degeneres animos' is the object of 'arguit' (proves, exposes), and 'degeneres' means 'unworthy of one's birth'. The thought is an argument: since he shows no fear, he cannot be of base stock.

sentences.t:
heu, quibus ille
iactatus fatis!
sentences.l:
ah, by what fates he
tossed!
sentences.i: ah, what fates have driven him to and fro!
sentences.n: 'quibus… fatis' is an ablative of means with 'iactatus', exclamatory: 'by what fates!' 'iactatus' is the perfect participle passive, 'tossed about', agreeing with 'ille' with 'est' left out. The word echoes the poem's own opening, where Aeneas is 'much tossed' ('iactatus').

sentences.t: Quae bella exhausta canebat!
sentences.l: What wars endured to the end he was telling!
sentences.i: What wars he told of, fought through to the end!
sentences.n: 'exhausta' is literally 'drained to the last drop', so endured right through. 'canebat' is the imperfect of 'cano', he used to tell, he kept telling: the reference is to the tale of Troy told in Books II–III.

sentences.i: If it were not settled in my mind, fixed and unshaken, that I should wish to join myself to no one in the bond of marriage, now that my first love has deceived and failed me by dying,
sentences.n: A long conditional that finishes at line 19. 'sederet' is imperfect subjunctive: a condition contrary to fact, 'if it were not settled'. Its subject is the whole clause 'ne cui… vellem', 'that I should wish to join myself to no one'; 'cui' is 'alicui' after 'ne'. 'vinclo iugali' is a bond of the yoke, marriage. 'postquam primus amor… fefellit' — 'fefellit' has 'me' for its object, with 'deceptam' agreeing: 'cheated me and left me deceived'. The first love is Sychaeus, her husband.

sentences.t:
si non pertaesum thalami taedaeque fuisset,
huic uni forsan potui succumbere culpae.
sentences.l:
if it had not been wearisome — of the marriage-chamber and the torch —
to this one failing perhaps I was able to yield.
sentences.i: and if I had not become weary of the marriage bed and its torch, then perhaps I could have yielded to this one weakness.
sentences.n: 'pertaesum fuisset' is impersonal, 'it had wearied (me)', with a genitive of the thing: 'thalami taedaeque', of the bridal chamber and the wedding torch. The conclusion is the indicative 'potui', 'I could have' (a verb of ability often stands in the indicative where English would say 'would'). 'succumbere' takes the dative 'culpae'. Dido already calls it a 'fault'.

sentences.t:
Anna, fatebor enim, miseri post fata Sychaei
coniugis et sparsos fraterna caede Penatis,
solus hic inflexit sensus, animumque labantem
impulit:
sentences.l:
Anna — for I shall confess — after the fates of wretched Sychaeus,
my husband, and the household gods spattered by a brother's slaughter,
this man alone has bent my feelings, and my wavering mind
has pushed:
sentences.i: Anna, I will confess it: since the death of my unhappy husband Sychaeus, and the household gods spattered by my brother's murder, this man alone has swayed my feelings and given my faltering heart its push:
sentences.n: 'fatebor enim' is a parenthesis, 'for I will confess'. 'miseri… Sychaei coniugis' — the husband is Sychaeus, murdered by Dido's brother Pygmalion at the altar (the story is told in Book I). 'fata' is his fate, his death. 'Penatis' is Greenough's accusative plural in '-is' (you'll see this constantly: 'omnis', 'montis'): the household gods, spattered with blood because the murder was done at the altar. 'solus hic' is the emphatic subject. 'animum labantem impulit' — a tottering mind given the push that sends it over.

sentences.t: adgnosco veteris vestigia flammae.
sentences.l: I recognise the footprints of an old flame.
sentences.i: I know again the tracks of a fire that once burned in me.
sentences.n: 'adgnosco' is Greenough's spelling of 'agnosco' (the Latin Library has the familiar form; same word). It is a compound of 'ad' and 'gnosco' (learn to know), so 'know again, recognise as one's own'. 'vestigia' means footprints, the tracks that a hunter follows; 'veteris flammae' is the old love, for Sychaeus. Love as flame is the book's metaphor and the same image appears in line 2; the footprints look ahead to the hunted doe at lines 69–73.

sentences.t:
Sed mihi vel tellus optem prius ima dehiscat,
vel Pater omnipotens adigat me fulmine ad umbras,
pallentis umbras Erebi noctemque profundam,
ante, Pudor, quam te violo, aut tua iura resolvo.
sentences.l:
But for me either earth, I would wish, first open to its depths,
or the Father almighty drive me with his thunderbolt to the shades,
the pale shades of Erebus and deep night,
before, Shame, I violate you, or loosen your laws.
sentences.i: But before I violate you, Shame, or break your laws, I pray that the earth may first open deep beneath me, or the Almighty Father drive me with his thunderbolt down to the shades, the pale shades of Erebus and bottomless night.
sentences.n: 'optem' (I would wish) is a parenthesis; the wishes themselves are the subjunctives 'dehiscat' and 'adigat', 'let the earth gape, let the Father drive'. 'mihi' is a dative of interest, 'for me'. 'Pater omnipotens' is Jupiter. 'pallentis' is the accusative plural in '-is', agreeing with 'umbras'. Erebus is the dark of the underworld. The Latin Library has 'Erebo' where Greenough has the genitive 'Erebi' ('the shades of Erebus'); either way the shades belong to the dark world below. 'Pudor' is personified Shame, here the sense of fidelity to the dead husband. 'ante… quam', 'before… than', is split by 'Pudor' and 'te'; 'violo' and 'resolvo' are present indicatives. 'iura resolvo' — loosen, undo, her obligations.

sentences.t:
Ille meos, primus qui me sibi iunxit, amores
abstulit;
sentences.l:
That man my loves, who first joined me to himself,
carried off;
sentences.i: He who first joined me to himself took my love away;
sentences.n: 'Ille' is Sychaeus. 'amores' is a plural of the abstract (love, affection). The relative clause 'primus qui me sibi iunxit' is placed inside the main clause, between 'meos' and 'amores'.

sentences.t: ille habeat secum servetque sepulchro.”
sentences.l: let him have them with himself and keep them in the tomb.”
sentences.i: let him keep it with him, and guard it in the grave.”
sentences.n: 'habeat servetque' are jussive subjunctives ('let him have and keep'). 'ille' is repeated for emphasis. 'sepulchro' is Greenough's spelling (the Latin Library has 'sepulcro'). Dido's speech ends here.

sentences.t: Sic effata sinum lacrimis implevit obortis.
sentences.l: So having spoken, her lap with tears she filled, arisen.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and filled the fold of her gown with welling tears.
sentences.n: 'effata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'effor', and so active in sense, 'having spoken'. 'sinum' is the fold of the dress over the breast. 'obortis' (ablative with 'lacrimis') means 'rising up, welling'.

sentences.t: Anna refert:
sentences.l: Anna replies:
sentences.i: Anna answers:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'refert' is a historic present introducing the reply. Anna's speech marks run to line 53.

sentences.t:
“O luce magis dilecta sorori,
solane perpetua maerens carpere iuventa,
nec dulcis natos, Veneris nec praemia noris?
sentences.l:
“O more dear than light to your sister,
will you alone, mourning, be worn away in perpetual youth,
and neither sweet children nor Venus's rewards know?
sentences.i: “O you who are dearer to your sister than the very light, will you let your youth be worn away in lonely grief, and never know sweet children or the rewards of love?
sentences.n: 'luce' is an ablative of comparison with 'magis dilecta': dearer than light. 'sorori' is the dative with 'dilecta', 'to your sister', Anna speaking of herself in the third person; 'dilecta' itself is a vocative addressed to Dido. 'solane' is 'sola' with the question-particle '-ne'. 'carpere' is the second person singular passive, the same as 'carperis': 'will you be worn away?', as in 'carpitur' at line 2 (the long -e- is what the metre needs; an infinitive would have a short one). 'dulcis' is the accusative plural in '-is', agreeing with 'natos'. 'noris' is the contracted form of 'noveris' (perfect subjunctive of 'nosco'). 'Veneris praemia' is love and its consequences.

sentences.t: Id cinerem aut Manis credis curare sepultos?
sentences.l: That ash or Shades do you believe care about, buried?
sentences.i: Do you think the ashes or the buried spirits care for that?
sentences.n: 'Id' is the object of 'curare'. 'cinerem' (singular) and 'Manis' are the accusative subjects of 'curare' after 'credis'; 'Manis' is the accusative plural in '-is' (Manes, the spirits of the dead), and 'sepultos' is 'buried', agreeing with it. Anna's argument is that the dead do not care about Dido's faithfulness.

sentences.t: Esto:
sentences.l: Be it so:
sentences.i: Granted:
sentences.n: 'esto' is the future imperative of 'sum': 'let it be so'; Anna concedes the point before a new objection.

sentences.t:
aegram nulli quondam flexere mariti,
non Libyae, non ante Tyro; despectus Iarbas
ductoresque alii, quos Africa terra triumphis
dives alit:
sentences.l:
sick at heart, no suitors once bent you,
not in Libya, not before in Tyre; Iarbas spurned,
and other chieftains, whom Africa, land
rich in triumphs, nourishes:
sentences.i: No suitor ever swayed you in your grief, neither in Libya nor earlier in Tyre; Iarbas was spurned, and the other chieftains whom Africa, a land rich in triumphs, breeds:
sentences.n: 'aegram' agrees with the 'te' left understood, 'you in your sickness of heart'. 'nulli… mariti' — 'maritus' is a husband, here a would-be husband, a suitor. 'flexere' is 'flexerunt' (the ending '-ere' for '-erunt'; you'll see it constantly). 'Libyae' (a locative) and 'Tyro' (an ablative) mean 'in Libya' and 'in Tyre'. 'despectus Iarbas' has 'est' omitted: Iarbas was spurned, a king of the neighbouring peoples whose name returns later in the book. 'triumphis dives' — rich in triumphs; the ablative goes with 'dives'.

sentences.t: placitone etiam pugnabis amori?
sentences.l: to a pleasing love even will you fight?
sentences.i: will you really struggle even against a love that pleases you?
sentences.n: 'placito… amori' is the dative after 'pugnabis' (fight against); 'placito' is the participle of 'placeo', 'that pleases'. The '-ne' makes the question; 'etiam' is 'even'.

sentences.t: Nec venit in mentem, quorum consederis arvis?
sentences.l: Nor does it come into your mind, in whose fields you have settled?
sentences.i: Does it not cross your mind in whose lands you have settled?
sentences.n: 'in mentem venit' is the idiom 'it comes to mind'. 'quorum… arvis' is an indirect question: 'in whose fields'. 'consederis' is perfect subjunctive of 'consido'. The peoples who surround the city are listed next.

sentences.t:
Hinc Gaetulae urbes, genus insuperabile bello,
et Numidae infreni cingunt et inhospita Syrtis;
sentences.l:
On this side Gaetulian cities, a race unconquerable in war,
and the unbridled Numidians surround you, and the inhospitable Syrtis;
sentences.i: On this side the Gaetulian cities, a race unconquerable in war, encircle you, with the unbridled Numidians and the inhospitable Syrtis;
sentences.n: 'cingunt' is one verb serving three subjects: the Gaetulian cities, the Numidians, and the Syrtis, the notorious shoals off the African coast. 'genus insuperabile bello' is in apposition: the Gaetulians are a race unconquerable 'in war' (ablative). 'infreni' is 'unbridled'. 'hinc… hinc' in the next line means 'on this side… on that'.

sentences.t:
hinc deserta siti regio, lateque furentes
Barcaei.
sentences.l:
on that side a region deserted by thirst, and far and wide raging
the Barcaeans.
sentences.i: on the other, a region desolate with drought, and the Barcaeans raging far and wide.
sentences.n: 'siti' is the ablative of 'sitis', thirst: a land left empty by drought. 'late' with 'furentes', raging far and wide. The Barcaeans are a people of Barca in Libya.

sentences.t:
Quid bella Tyro surgentia dicam,
germanique minas?
sentences.l:
Why should I mention wars from Tyre arising,
and your brother's threats?
sentences.i: Why should I speak of the wars now rising out of Tyre, and of your brother's threats?
sentences.n: 'Quid… dicam' is a deliberative subjunctive: 'what am I to say of…?' 'Tyro' is ablative, 'out of Tyre'; the brother is Pygmalion, who murdered Sychaeus. Line 44 stops after 'germanique minas?': it is one of the unfinished half-lines Virgil left in the poem, and the sense is complete at the break.

sentences.t:
Dis equidem auspicibus reor et Iunone secunda
hunc cursum Iliacas vento tenuisse carinas.
sentences.l:
With gods as auspices, I think indeed, and with Juno favourable,
this course the Ilian keels by the wind have held.
sentences.i: I truly believe it was by the gods' auspices, and with Juno's favour, that the Trojan ships held to this course before the wind.
sentences.n: 'Dis auspicibus' and 'Iunone secunda' are ablative absolutes with no participle (the verb 'sum' has no present participle): 'the gods being the guides, Juno being favourable'. 'reor' is the deponent 'I think'. 'tenuisse' is the infinitive in accusative and infinitive: the ships kept this course. 'Iliacas' is Trojan (Ilium). 'secunda' literally means 'following', hence favouring. Juno is in fact the Trojans' bitter enemy, and Anna is wrong; the irony is Virgil's.

sentences.t:
Quam tu urbem, soror, hanc cernes, quae surgere regna
coniugio tali!
sentences.l:
What city, sister, this one will you see, what kingdoms to rise
from such a marriage!
sentences.i: Sister, what a city you will see here, and what kingdoms rising, with such a marriage!
sentences.n: 'Quam urbem… cernes' is exclamatory: 'what a city!'; 'quae… regna' is another exclamation, and 'cernes' takes the accusative and infinitive 'regna surgere', 'kingdoms rising'. 'coniugio tali' — an ablative of means or circumstance: 'by such a union'. 'coniugio' has a consonantal i in the middle: con-yu-gio.

sentences.t:
Teucrum comitantibus armis
Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus!
sentences.l:
With Teucrians' arms accompanying,
Punic glory itself with how great deeds will lift up!
sentences.i: With Trojan arms beside her own, how high will Punic glory raise itself, and by what mighty deeds!
sentences.n: 'Teucrum' is the old genitive plural for 'Teucrorum' (you'll see this constantly: 'virum', 'divom'). 'Teucri' is Trojans, from their early king Teucer. 'comitantibus armis' is an ablative absolute. 'Punica gloria' is Carthaginian glory (Punic is from the Latin for Phoenician). 'se attollet' is 'will raise itself'. 'quantis rebus' is an ablative of means with exclamatory 'quantis': by what great deeds. The Carthage of the future that Anna imagines is one the Romans would remember as their great enemy.

sentences.t:
Tu modo posce deos veniam, sacrisque litatis
indulge hospitio, causasque innecte morandi,
dum pelago desaevit hiemps et aquosus Orion,
quassataeque rates, dum non tractabile caelum.”
sentences.l:
You only ask the gods for favour, and the sacrifices having been favourable,
indulge hospitality, and weave causes of delaying,
while on the sea rages out the storm and rainy Orion,
and the ships are battered, while the sky is not to be handled.”
sentences.i: Only beg the gods for their favour, and when the offerings have won good omens, give yourself to hospitality and tie together reasons for delay, while winter rages on the sea, and rainy Orion, and the ships lie battered, while the sky cannot be dealt with.”
sentences.n: 'modo' with an imperative means 'only'. 'sacris litatis' is an ablative absolute: 'litare' is to sacrifice with favourable omens, so 'the sacrifices having been accepted'. 'indulge hospitio' — give way to, 'indulge in', with the dative. 'morandi' is the gerund in the genitive, 'of delaying'. 'dum… desaevit' is a present indicative with 'dum', 'while'. 'hiemps' is Greenough's spelling of 'hiems', winter, storm. The constellation Orion was associated with stormy weather. 'non tractabile' is 'not to be handled, unmanageable'. Anna's speech ends here.

sentences.t:
His dictis incensum animum inflammavit amore,
spemque dedit dubiae menti, solvitque pudorem.
sentences.l:
By these words her kindled mind she inflamed with love,
and hope she gave to her doubtful mind, and loosed her shame.
sentences.i: With these words she set Dido's kindled heart ablaze with love; she gave hope to a wavering mind and loosed the hold of shame.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. The subject is Anna, unnamed. Greenough prints 'incensum animum inflammavit amore': 'she inflamed the already kindled mind'. The Latin Library has instead 'impenso animum flammavit amore', 'she set the mind aflame with intense love'; the sense differs only in emphasis, whether the mind was already burning or the love is intense. 'dubiae menti' is a dative, 'to a doubting mind'. 'solvit pudorem' — loosed her shame, undid the scruple Dido had named 'Pudor' at line 27.

sentences.t:
Principio delubra adeunt, pacemque per aras
exquirunt;
sentences.l:
First the shrines they approach, and peace through the altars
they seek;
sentences.i: First they go to the shrines and seek the gods' goodwill at the altars;
sentences.n: The subject, 'they', is the two sisters, not named. 'adeunt' and 'exquirunt' are present tenses in the narrative. 'pacem' here is the favour of the gods, which sacrifice seeks. 'principio' is an adverbial ablative, 'at the start'.

sentences.t:
mactant lectas de more bidentis
legiferae Cereri Phoeboque patrique Lyaeo,
Iunoni ante omnis, cui vincla iugalia curae.
sentences.l:
they slay chosen sheep according to custom
to law-giving Ceres and to Phoebus and to Father Lyaeus,
to Juno before all, to whom the bonds of marriage are a care.
sentences.i: they slay chosen sheep, as custom requires, to Ceres the lawgiver, to Phoebus, and to Father Lyaeus, and above all to Juno, whose care is the bonds of marriage.
sentences.n: 'bidentis' is the accusative plural in '-is' of 'bidens', a sheep of two years, the usual sacrificial animal. 'de more' is 'according to custom'. 'legiferae Cereri' — Ceres the lawgiver, patron of settled civic life. 'Lyaeus' is a name of Bacchus. 'ante omnis' is 'before all' (accusative plural in '-is'). 'cui vincla iugalia curae' is a double dative with 'est' left out: 'to whom the marriage bonds are a care'. Juno, patron of marriage, is the very goddess who will be at work against the Trojans.

sentences.t:
Ipsa, tenens dextra pateram, pulcherrima Dido
candentis vaccae media inter cornua fundit,
aut ante ora deum pinguis spatiatur ad aras,
instauratque diem donis, pecudumque reclusis
pectoribus inhians spirantia consulit exta.
sentences.l:
She herself, holding a bowl in her right hand, fairest Dido,
of a shining cow between the middle horns pours,
or before the faces of the gods to the fat altars paces,
and renews the day with gifts, and, of the beasts opened
breasts gazing, the breathing entrails consults.
sentences.i: Dido herself, loveliest of women, holds the bowl in her right hand and pours the wine between the horns of a gleaming white cow, or walks before the gods' faces to the rich altars; she renews the day with gifts, and, bending eagerly over the opened breasts of the victims, consults the quivering entrails.
sentences.n: A five-line sentence of ritual. 'patera' is the shallow libation bowl. 'candentis vaccae' is genitive, 'of a gleaming white cow'; 'media inter cornua' — 'inter' stands between its adjective and its noun, 'between the horns'. 'deum' is 'deorum' (the old short genitive plural). 'pinguis' is the accusative plural in '-is', agreeing with 'aras'. 'instaurat diem donis' — 'instaurat' is to renew, to do over again; 'instaurat diem donis' is 'she renews the day with gifts', most likely that she keeps the day's worship going with fresh offerings. 'pecudum reclusis pectoribus' is an ablative absolute, 'the breasts of the beasts having been opened'. 'inhians' is gaping at, gazing eagerly. 'spirantia exta' — the entrails still seem to breathe; they were read for omens.

sentences.t: Heu vatum ignarae mentes!
sentences.l: Alas, of seers the ignorant minds!
sentences.i: Alas, how blind are the minds of seers!
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and the narrator breaks in with a comment of his own. 'vatum' is the genitive plural of 'vates', seer or prophet; 'ignarae' (ignorant, blind) agrees with 'mentes', so 'the ignorant minds of seers'. The words can also be taken as 'minds ignorant of seers', with 'ignarae' governing 'vatum'; the first is the reading used here. The reader knows how the story ends and the soothsayers here do not.

sentences.t:
quid vota furentem,
quid delubra iuvant?
sentences.l:
what vows a raging woman,
what shrines help?
sentences.i: What can vows do for a woman in her frenzy, what can shrines?
sentences.n: 'iuvant' takes 'furentem' (the raving Dido) as its object, with 'quid' an adverbial 'what good?'. The rhetorical question is the narrator's. 'delubra' is the word for shrines at line 56.

sentences.t:
Est mollis flamma medullas
interea, et tacitum vivit sub pectore volnus.
sentences.l:
Eats a soft flame the marrow meanwhile,
and silent lives under her breast the wound.
sentences.i: Meanwhile a gentle flame eats at her marrow, and the silent wound lives on beneath her heart.
sentences.n: 'Est' here is not 'is' but the contracted present of 'edo', to eat (the same as 'edit'), with 'medullas' as its object. 'mollis' can be read with 'flamma' (a soft flame) or with 'medullas' (soft marrow; accusative plural in '-is'); the sense is a love that eats into her without outward sign. 'tacitum… volnus' picks up 'volnus' of line 2: the poem has come round to its opening image.

sentences.t:
Uritur infelix Dido, totaque vagatur
urbe furens, qualis coniecta cerva sagitta,
quam procul incautam nemora inter Cresia fixit
pastor agens telis, liquitque volatile ferrum
nescius;
sentences.l:
Burns unhappy Dido, and through all the city
wanders raging, like a doe struck by an arrow,
whom from afar unwary among Cretan woods a shepherd
has pierced, pursuing with darts, and has left the winged iron
unknowing;
sentences.i: Unhappy Dido burns, and wanders raging through the whole city, like a doe struck by an arrow, which a shepherd, chasing her with his darts, has pierced from afar as she was unwary in the woods of Crete, and left the winged iron in her, not knowing it;
sentences.n: 'Uritur' is passive of 'uro', 'is burned', so 'she burns'. The simile begins at 'qualis': 'like a doe'. 'coniecta sagitta' is 'struck by an arrow' (ablative of means). 'quam' is the doe, object of 'fixit'. 'nemora inter' — 'inter' after its noun. 'Cresia' is Cretan (Crete was famed for archers). 'pastor agens telis' — a shepherd hunting her with darts. 'volatile ferrum' is the arrow, called the winged iron by metonymy of the material. 'nescius' agrees with 'pastor': he does not know he has hit her. The simile sets the image for what follows: the unaware hunter is Aeneas, the wounded doe is Dido.

sentences.t:
illa fuga silvas saltusque peragrat
Dictaeos;
sentences.l:
she in flight woods and glades roams over
of Dicte;
sentences.i: she in her flight ranges through the woods and glades of Dicte;
sentences.n: 'illa' is the doe. 'peragrat' (ranges over) governs 'silvas saltusque'; 'Dictaeos' is masculine, agreeing with 'saltus' and serving for 'silvas' too: 'of Mount Dicte', a mountain in Crete.

sentences.t: haeret lateri letalis arundo.
sentences.l: clings to her flank the deadly reed.
sentences.i: the shaft that will kill her clings to her flank.
sentences.n: 'haeret lateri' — 'sticks to the flank', with the dative. 'arundo' is a reed, hence an arrow-shaft by metonymy (the Latin Library prints it 'harundo'; same word). 'letalis' is deadly.

sentences.t:
Nunc media Aenean secum per moenia ducit,
Sidoniasque ostentat opes urbemque paratam;
sentences.l:
Now through the middle walls Aeneas with her she leads,
and Sidonian wealth she shows and the city ready;
sentences.i: Now she leads Aeneas with her through the heart of the city walls, and shows him the wealth of Sidon and the city made ready for him;
sentences.n: 'media… moenia' — 'media' agrees with 'moenia': through the midst of the walls. 'Aenean' is the Greek-style accusative singular. 'Sidonias' is Sidonian, which here simply means Phoenician or Carthaginian (Sidon was the neighbour of Tyre). 'paratam' is 'prepared, ready'. The present tenses start a run of repeated, habitual actions.

sentences.t: incipit effari, mediaque in voce resistit;
sentences.l: she begins to speak out, and in the middle of the voice stops;
sentences.i: she begins to speak, and halts in the middle of her words;
sentences.n: 'effari' is the infinitive of the deponent 'effor', to speak out. 'media in voce' — in the middle of the utterance, as her voice fails.

sentences.t:
nunc eadem labente die convivia quaerit,
Iliacosque iterum demens audire labores
exposcit, pendetque iterum narrantis ab ore.
sentences.l:
now the same, with the day sinking, banquets she seeks,
and the Ilian toils again, out of her mind, to hear
she demands, and hangs again from the mouth of the teller.
sentences.i: Now, as the day wanes, she seeks the same feasts again, and, beside herself, begs to hear once more of the toils of Troy, and hangs again on the lips of the one who tells them.
sentences.n: 'eadem… convivia' — the same banquets as before, 'eadem' is neuter plural. 'labente die' is an ablative absolute, 'as the day slips away'. 'demens' is out of her mind. 'exposcit' is an urgent demand. 'narrantis' is the present participle in the genitive, 'of the one telling'. 'pendet ab ore' — hangs from his lips. 'Iliacos' is Trojan, 'labores' toils.

sentences.t:
Post, ubi digressi, lumenque obscura vicissim
luna premit suadentque cadentia sidera somnos,
sola domo maeret vacua, stratisque relictis
incubat, illum absens absentem auditque videtque;
sentences.l:
Afterwards, when they have parted, and the dim moon in turn
presses down the light and the setting stars counsel sleep,
alone in the empty house she grieves, and on the couch left behind
she lies, absent herself, him absent both hears and sees;
sentences.i: Afterwards, when the guests have parted, and the dim moon in her turn dims the light and the setting stars invite sleep, she grieves alone in the empty house and lies upon the deserted couch, hearing him and seeing him, each of them absent from the other;
sentences.n: 'ubi digressi' is 'when they have parted', with 'sunt' left out. 'obscura luna' — the moon, dim in her turn, 'vicissim'. 'suadent… somnos' — the stars persuade, counsel, sleep. 'sola… vacua' — the house is empty, she alone. 'stratisque relictis incubat' — 'incubat' takes the dative: she lies on the couches left behind, 'relictis' meaning left empty, deserted. 'illum absens absentem': 'absens' is she, absent, and 'absentem' is him, absent, either side of 'illum', the object of 'auditque videtque': she hears and sees him though each is away from the other.

sentences.t:
aut gremio Ascanium, genitoris imagine capta,
detinet, infandum si fallere possit amorem.
sentences.l:
or in her lap Ascanius, by his father's image captured,
she holds, if she might deceive the unspeakable love.
sentences.i: Or, captivated by the likeness of his father, she holds Ascanius in her lap, in case she might cheat the love she cannot speak of.
sentences.n: 'capta' agrees with Dido, the subject (not with Ascanius): she is caught by the boy's resemblance to his father. 'gremio' is an ablative of place, in her lap. 'infandum' is literally 'not to be spoken', unspeakable. 'si fallere possit' — 'if she might be able to deceive', that is, in the hope of cheating the love; a 'si' clause with the subjunctive, 'to see whether she can'.

sentences.i: The towers begun do not rise, the young men no longer drill in arms, nor do they make ready harbours or bulwarks to be safe in war;
sentences.n: 'coeptae turres' — the begun towers. 'adsurgunt' is Greenough's spelling, rise up. 'iuventus' is a collective singular (the young men): the verb is singular in 'exercet' and plural in 'parant', where the meaning is plural, so the subject of 'parant' is again 'iuventus'. 'portusve aut propugnacula' — harbours and bulwarks. 'tuta bello' is 'safe in war' or 'for war', with 'bello' ablative (or dative).

sentences.t:
pendent opera interrupta, minaeque
murorum ingentes aequataque machina caelo.
sentences.l:
hang the works interrupted, and the threats
of walls huge and the engine levelled with the sky.
sentences.i: The works hang broken off, the huge threatening walls, and the crane raised to match the sky.
sentences.n: 'pendent opera interrupta' — the works hang interrupted, broken off. 'minae murorum ingentes' — the threats of the walls, an idiom for walls that loom threateningly. 'machina' is a hoisting engine or crane. 'aequata caelo' is 'made level with the sky' (dative). The picture is of a city stopped in mid-construction.

sentences.t:
Quam simul ac tali persensit peste teneri
cara Iovis coniunx, nec famam obstare furori,
talibus adgreditur Venerem Saturnia dictis:
sentences.l:
Whom as soon as she perceived to be held by such a plague,
dear wife of Jove, and no repute to stand in the way of the madness,
with such words approaches Venus Saturn's daughter:
sentences.i: As soon as Jove's dear wife saw that Dido was gripped by such a plague, and that her good name stood no longer in the way of her madness, Saturn's daughter accosted Venus with these words:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Quam' is a connecting relative, 'her' (Dido), the first word of the sentence in place of 'et eam'. 'persensit' governs two accusatives and infinitives: 'teneri' (that she was held) and 'famam obstare' (that repute stood in the way). 'fama' is her good name or reputation. 'cara Iovis coniunx' and 'Saturnia' both mean Juno (Saturn was her father). 'adgreditur' is a historic present, 'accosts'.

sentences.t:
“Egregiam vero laudem et spolia ampla refertis
tuque puerque tuus, magnum et memorabile numen,
una dolo divom si femina victa duorum est!
sentences.l:
“Egregious praise indeed and ample spoils you bring back,
you and your boy, great and memorable divinity,
if one woman by the guile of two gods is conquered!
sentences.i: “Noble praise indeed, and ample spoils, do you carry home, you and that boy of yours — what a great and memorable power! — if one woman has been beaten by the trickery of two gods!
sentences.n: Juno's speech opens (the marks run to line 104). She is speaking with sarcasm. 'refertis' is 'you bring back', as of a victory. 'tuque puerque tuus' — 'you and your boy', Venus and Cupid, who disguised himself as Ascanius in Book I so as to kindle Dido. 'magnum et memorabile numen' is bitterly in apposition. 'divom duorum' — 'divom' is the old genitive plural of 'divus', Greenough's spelling (the Latin Library prints it 'diuum'; same word), of two gods. 'victa est' is the perfect passive: she has been conquered.

sentences.t:
Nec me adeo fallit veritam te moenia nostra
suspectas habuisse domos Karthaginis altae.
sentences.l:
Nor does it escape me that you, fearing, my walls
have held suspect, the houses of high Carthage.
sentences.i: Nor does it escape me that you, in your fear, regarded my walls with suspicion, the homes of high Carthage.
sentences.n: 'Nec me adeo fallit' takes an accusative and infinitive: 'te… habuisse', that you held. 'veritam' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'vereor', 'fearing'. 'adeo' strengthens the negative: 'not indeed'. 'suspectas habuisse' — 'to have held suspect'. 'domos' is an accusative plural in apposition to 'moenia'. 'Karthaginis' is Greenough's spelling. Carthage is Juno's own city; she calls the walls 'nostra'.

sentences.t: Sed quis erit modus, aut quo nunc certamine tanto?
sentences.l: But what will be the limit, or to what contest now so great?
sentences.i: But what limit will there be, or what is the point of so great a contest now?
sentences.n: 'quo… certamine tanto' is a question with the verb left out: to what end such a contest? The rhetorical question begins her offer.

sentences.t:
Quin potius pacem aeternam pactosque hymenaeos
exercemus?
sentences.l:
Why not rather peace eternal and pledged marriage
let us work at?
sentences.i: Why do we not rather set about an everlasting peace and a pledged marriage?
sentences.n: 'Quin' with the present indicative 'exercemus' makes an urging question: 'why do we not…?' 'exerceo' is to keep at work, to practise. 'hymenaeos' is the Greek accusative plural, wedding rites. 'pactos' is 'agreed', 'pledged'. Juno puts her proposal of a joint settlement as a question.

sentences.t: Habes, tota quod mente petisti:
sentences.l: You have what with your whole mind you sought:
sentences.i: You have what you sought with your whole heart:
sentences.n: 'Habes' is the indicative: you have, you have gained. 'petisti' is a contracted perfect for 'petivisti' (a contraction you will meet often). The colon introduces the proof.

sentences.t: ardet amans Dido, traxitque per ossa furorem.
sentences.l: burns loving Dido, and has drawn through her bones the madness.
sentences.i: Dido burns with love, and has drawn the frenzy deep into her bones.
sentences.n: 'ardet amans' — 'amans' is the participle of 'amo', 'loving', in apposition to 'Dido'. 'traxit… furorem' — has drawn the madness through her bones, the verb a perfect. The words 'ardet' and 'furorem' pick up 'uritur' and 'furens' of lines 68–69.

sentences.t:
Communem hunc ergo populum paribusque regamus
auspiciis;
sentences.l:
In common this people then, and with equal
auspices let us rule;
sentences.i: Let us then rule this people jointly, under equal auspices;
sentences.n: 'regamus' is a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us rule'. 'communem hunc populum' — framing 'ergo', 'then'. 'paribus auspiciis' is an ablative of attendant circumstances, with the same authority. 'auspicia' are the right to take omens and so to command.

sentences.t:
liceat Phrygio servire marito,
dotalisque tuae Tyrios permittere dextrae.”
sentences.l:
let it be allowed to serve a Phrygian husband,
and as dowry to your right hand the Tyrians to entrust.”
sentences.i: let her be permitted to serve a Phrygian husband, and to hand over the Tyrians to your keeping as a dowry.”
sentences.n: 'liceat' is a jussive subjunctive, 'let it be allowed', with the infinitives 'servire' (taking the dative 'Phrygio marito') and 'permittere' (with 'dextrae'). 'Phrygio' is Trojan; the Trojans are often called Phrygians in the Aeneid. 'dotalis' is the accusative plural in '-is' agreeing with 'Tyrios': 'as a dowry'. 'dextrae' is the right hand, here the power of Venus. The speech ends, and the part with it.
